# Wire drawing (`wire_drawing`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/manufacturing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Tools, machines & manufacturing (`manufacturing`)
- Deps: needs bloomery_iron; helped by crucible_steel, water_wheel
- Core idea: Point the end of a soft metal rod, push it through a tapered hole in a hard steel plate (the drawplate) and pull the rest through with tongs, a windlass or a water-driven crank; it comes out thinner, longer and exactly round. Repeat through a row of holes each about a tenth smaller in diameter. Drawing hardens the metal, so after a few passes the wire must be annealed (heated to red and cooled slowly) or it snaps. Grease, wax or soap in the hole is essential. Wire makes pins, needles, nails, mail armour, card teeth for wool, springs, strings and later cables and telegraph lines.
- Pitfalls:
  - Too big a reduction per pass, or no annealing: the wire breaks
  - Dry drawing; the wire welds to the plate and scores
  - Iron with slag threads in it splits in the plate; wire needs the cleanest iron
  - Brass and iron wire need different annealing; brass must not be worked hot
- History: mesopotamia: 3rd millennium BC – gold wire made by hammering and by twisting cut strips (Ur); egypt: 2nd millennium BC – strip-twisted and hammered wire in jewellery; true drawing in antiquity is not proven; europe: 8th–10th c. – iron drawplates in Viking-age finds; c. 1122 Theophilus describes the drawplate; c. 1350–1415 water-powered wire mills at Nuremberg; 1540 Biringuccio illustrates them; islamic: early medieval – drawn gold and silver wire for textiles; dates uncertain
- Read:
  - Theophilus, On Divers Arts (c. 1122; tr. J. G. Hawthorne & C. S. Smith, 1963)
  - W. A. Oddy, The Production of Gold Wire in Antiquity, Gold Bulletin 10 (1977)
  - Vannoccio Biringuccio, De la pirotechnia (1540; tr. C. S. Smith & M. T. Gnudi, 1942)
